The thought of the Widow Douglas's generous hospitality was hard to resist. Together with Tom's persuasion, it soon settled the matter. They decided to tell nobody about their plans for the night. Then Tom suddenly remembered that Huck might come that very evening and give the signal. The thought spoiled much of his excitement. Yet he could not bear to miss the fun at the widow's house. Why should he, he argued with himself? There had been no signal the night before. Why was one any more likely tonight? The evening's certain pleasure mattered more than the uncertain treasure. Like a boy, he gave in to the stronger temptation and decided not to think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferry stopped and tied up at the entrance to a wooded valley. Everyone hurried ashore. Soon shouts and laughter echoed through the forest and around the rocky heights. They tried every possible way of getting hot and tired. At last the wanderers drifted back to camp with impressive appetites, and the good food began to disappear. After the meal came a pleasant rest, with conversation in the shade of the spreading oaks. Then someone called out:

“Who's ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. They collected bundles of candles and raced up the hill. The cave entrance, shaped like the letter A, stood partway up the hillside. Its massive oak door was unbarred. Inside lay a small chamber as cold as an icehouse, with solid limestone walls wet as though with a cold sweat. Standing in its deep darkness and looking out at the sunlit green valley felt romantic and mysterious. But that sense of wonder quickly faded, and the rough play started again. Whenever someone lit a candle, everyone rushed at its owner. A struggle followed, with a brave attempt to defend the light, but soon the candle was knocked down or blown out. Laughter burst out, and another chase began. Yet everything ends eventually. Before long they formed a line and started down the steep main passage. Their flickering candles dimly lit the high rock walls almost to the point where they met sixty feet overhead. The main passage was only eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other tall, even narrower cracks branched away to the left and right. McDougal's cave was an enormous maze of twisting passages that crossed, joined, and separated again, leading nowhere.

She was right about the rats. Every so often one poked its nose out of a hole in the corner. She said that when she was alone, she needed things close by to throw at them, or they wouldn't leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot. Usually she could throw it accurately, she said, but she had strained her arm a day or two earlier and didn't know how well she could aim now. She waited for a chance and threw it at a rat, but missed by a long way. Her arm hurt so much that she cried, “Ouch!” Then she told me to try at the next one. I wanted to leave before her husband returned, though of course I didn't say so. I took the lead and hurled it at the first rat that showed its nose. If it had stayed still, it would have been a pretty sick rat. She said that was excellent and thought I'd hit the next one. She fetched the lead and brought back a loop of yarn for me to help with. I held up both hands, and she slipped the yarn around them. Then she kept talking about herself and her husband until she paused to say:

“Watch for the rats. You'd better keep the lead in your lap where you can reach it.”

Just then she dropped it into my lap. I pressed my legs together to catch it, and she continued talking—but only for about a minute. Then she lifted off the yarn and looked pleasantly but directly into my face.

“Come on, now. What's your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma'am?”

“Your real name. Is it Bill, Tom, Bob—or something else?”

I must have trembled like a leaf. I hardly knew what to do, but I said:

“Please don't make fun of a poor girl like me, ma'am. If I'm in your way, I'll—”

“No, you won't. Sit down and stay there. I'm not going to hurt you or tell anyone about you. Just trust me and tell me your secret. I'll keep it, and I'll help you too. So will my husband, if you want him to. You're an apprentice who's run away, that's all. It's nothing serious. There's no harm in it. They treated you badly, and you decided to leave. Bless you, child, I wouldn't give you away.

I then bored a hole in the end of the keg above the pitcher and inserted a plug of soft wood carved into a tapering cone. I pushed it in or drew it out as necessary, experimenting until it fitted with precisely the tightness required. Water seeping through the hole would then fall into the pitcher below and fill it to the brim in exactly sixty minutes. This was naturally quick and easy to establish by measuring what proportion of the pitcher filled within a given time. Once that was arranged, the rest of the plan was straightforward. I positioned my bed on the basket floor so that, when I lay down, my head would rest directly beneath the pitcher's spout. Clearly, after an hour, the full pitcher would have to overflow, and the water would escape through the spout, which sat slightly below the rim. Just as clearly, falling more than four feet, that water could only land on my face. The inevitable result would be to wake me instantly, even from the soundest possible sleep.

“It was already eleven when I finished these arrangements, and I went straight to bed, entirely confident that my invention would work. That confidence was justified. Exactly every sixty minutes, my dependable timekeeper woke me. I poured the pitcher's contents back into the keg through its bung-hole, performed the necessary work on the condenser, and lay down again. These regular interruptions disturbed my sleep even less than I had expected. When I finally rose for the day, it was seven o'clock, and the sun stood many degrees above the line of my horizon.

“April 3. I found the balloon at an enormous altitude, with the earth's curvature noticeably more pronounced. Beneath me, a group of black specks lay in the ocean, undoubtedly islands. Far north, at the edge of the horizon, I noticed a narrow white streak of extraordinary brilliance. I had no hesitation in identifying it as the southern edge of the Polar Sea's ice. This greatly excited my curiosity, since I hoped to travel much farther north and might eventually find myself directly above the Pole itself. I regretted that, if this happened, my immense height would prevent me from making as precise a survey as I would have liked.
